warmup.q: Two regions each run a leader for the same payments table and replicate to each other asynchronously, usually within a second. A checkout times out, and the client retries in the other region 200 ms later with the same idempotency key. Each region charges the card only if its INSERT of the key succeeds against a unique index. How many charges?
options: One: the unique index rejects the second insert
Two, if the retry lands before the first insert has replicated: each region checks the key against its own copy
One: asynchronous replication always delivers the first insert before the second region commits
None: the two inserts conflict and both roll back
warmup.why: Each leader enforces the unique index on its own copy of the table. With replication lag of up to a second, the second region hasn't seen the first key 200 ms later, so its insert succeeds too, and both regions charge. The index is real, and it is checked against an incomplete copy. When the two inserts later meet, the conflict rule (often last write wins) keeps one row, but the card was charged twice. Nothing rolls anything back, because each commit was already acknowledged.

sections.h: One leader per region keeps writes local, and lets two regions write the same row
sections.html:
A card terminal in Frankfurt places an authorization hold for merchant M-0042. If the only leader is in Virginia, the write crosses the Atlantic and comes back before the terminal hears OK: about 70 ms for one round trip, and 280 ms for a transaction of four statements that each wait for an answer. When the transatlantic link fails, or the Virginia region does, Frankfurt can't write at all until someone fails over, with the risks lesson 1 described.

The simplest fix is a leader in each region. The Frankfurt leader (call the region eu) commits its own clients' writes and answers in about a millisecond. The Virginia leader (us) does the same for its clients. Each leader also ships its replication log to the other, the logical row changes from lesson 2, and applies the other's log the way a follower would. So every region is a leader for its own clients and a follower of every other leader.

The copying has to be asynchronous. If eu waited for us before answering, every commit would pay the 70 ms again, and a broken link would stop writes in both regions. That's a single leader with extra parts.

Three kinds of system end up with this shape. Several regions, as here. Devices that keep working offline: a laptop on a train is a region whose replication lag is two hours, which is lesson 6. And collaborative editing, where each person's keystrokes apply to their own copy before any server has seen them.

The new problem fits in two writes. At 10:00:00.000 the eu leader adds hold h-eu to M-0042's open holds and acknowledges it. Ten milliseconds later, before that change has crossed the ocean, the us leader adds h-us to its own copy and acknowledges that. Both clients were told OK. Now each region holds a version of the row that the other has never seen. That's a write conflict, and when the changes arrive, each leader must do something with a row that doesn't match what it expected.

Conflicts aren't the only cost. Any rule that has to see every write stops working: a unique idempotency key, a balance that must stay at zero or above. Each leader checks the rule against its own copy, and both copies can pass. Inside one data center, where a round trip takes about half a millisecond, a second leader buys almost nothing for these costs, so multi-leader is a tool for regions and for offline devices.

Each region is a leader with its own log of writes, and the leaders copy each other's logs a few tens of milliseconds late. A conflict is a row for which two logs each hold a write the other hasn't seen. The rest of the lesson asks how the logs travel, and what to do when they disagree.

try.title: Two acknowledged writes, one survivor
steps: Read FirstConflictDemo.kt. It prints a timeline with one leader in us, then with a leader in each region, 35 ms apart one way.
Predict which hold survives last write wins, then run it from the labs folder. No Docker needed.
Change the us write's timestamp from 10 to -5, as if the us clock ran 15 ms behind, and run it again. Predict the survivor first.
try.expect:
-- one leader, in us --
t=0    eu  client sends: add hold h-eu
t=35   us  leader commits [h-eu]
t=70   eu  client gets OK after 70 ms; a 4-statement transaction would wait 280 ms

-- a leader in each region --
t=0    eu  leader commits [h-eu] at ts 0, client gets OK after 1 ms
t=10   us  leader commits [h-us] at ts 10, client gets OK after 1 ms
t=35   us  receives [h-eu] from eu; its own [h-us] never saw it: a conflict
t=45   eu  receives [h-us] from us; its own [h-eu] never saw it: a conflict

last write wins keeps ts 10 from us:  eu = [h-us]   us = [h-us]
acknowledged: h-eu, h-us   kept: [h-us]   lost: [h-eu]

Both clients heard OK after 1 ms, and both regions end with the same value, so replication "worked". One acknowledged hold is gone, and no one was told. With the us timestamp at -5 the last two lines become keeps ts 0 from eu and lost: [h-us]: the write made second now loses, because a clock decided, not the order of events.

sections.h: Topologies: circles, stars and all-to-all, and the update that overtakes its insert
sections.html:
With two leaders, each sends its log to the other. With three or more, someone has to decide who sends to whom, and there are three common shapes. In a circle, each leader forwards to the next one: eu to us, us to ap, ap back to eu, so a change reaches the far side by hopping through the others. In a star, one hub receives every leader's changes and forwards them to the rest. In all-to-all, every leader sends its changes straight to every other.

Forwarding creates a loop problem at once. If us forwards everything it applies, eu's change comes back to eu, which forwards it again, forever. So every change carries the id of the leader where it was first written (in a circle or a star, also the ids of the nodes it has passed through), and a node drops a change it has already applied. PostgreSQL's logical replication records the origin of every change it applies, and a subscription created with origin = none asks the publisher for local changes only, so two servers can subscribe to each other without echoing.

Circles and stars each depend on single nodes. A dead hub stops all replication; a dead node in a circle cuts the chain until someone rewires it. All-to-all has no such node, which is why it's the usual choice. Its weakness is quieter: changes take different links at different speeds, so a later change can overtake an earlier one.

The stepper shows a real case. eu inserts payment pay-81723 as AUTHORIZED. us gets the insert after 40 ms and captures the payment at 45 ms, an UPDATE to CAPTURED. Today ap's link from eu is slow, 150 ms, while us reaches ap in 30 ms. So ap gets the UPDATE at 75 ms, for a row it doesn't have yet. pgactive, AWS's active-active extension for PostgreSQL, documents its default for exactly this: discard the UPDATE. Its docs warn that this "can result in data inconsistencies across nodes". When the insert lands at 150 ms, ap says AUTHORIZED, the others say CAPTURED, and nothing will ever repair it.

Timestamps don't fix it. Suppose every leader keeps whichever version carries the later timestamp. If us's clock runs 60 ms behind eu's, the capture is stamped before the insert, and every region throws the capture away. The regions agree, on the wrong answer.

What works is to carry causality instead of time. The update records what us had applied when it made the change: eu's change number 1. ap holds the update until it has applied that change too, then applies both in order. That record, one counter per leader, is a version vector. Lesson 8 builds it properly.

stepper.title: An update overtakes its insert in all-to-all replication
stepper.intro: Three regions, each a leader, every leader sending to every other. Watch ap.

try.title: Three ways to treat an update that arrives early
steps: Read the delays at the top of OvertakeDemo.kt, then predict the final line of each of the three runs: discard, timestamps with us 60 ms behind, and causal.
In main, change run("timestamps", -60) to run("timestamps", 60) and run it again. Timestamps now give the right answer. Ask yourself what made the difference.
try.expect:
-- discard --
  t=0   eu applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=40  us applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=45  us applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  t=75  ap discards UPDATE CAPTURED: no such row
  t=85  eu applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  t=150 ap applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  final: eu=CAPTURED  us=CAPTURED  ap=AUTHORIZED

-- timestamps, us clock -60 ms off --
  t=0   eu applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=40  us applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=45  us ignores UPDATE CAPTURED: ts -15 < 0
  t=75  ap applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  t=85  eu ignores UPDATE CAPTURED: ts -15 < 0
  t=150 ap applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  final: eu=AUTHORIZED  us=AUTHORIZED  ap=AUTHORIZED

-- causal --
  t=0   eu applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=40  us applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=45  us applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  t=75  ap holds UPDATE CAPTURED: it needs {eu=1} first
  t=85  eu applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  t=150 ap applies INSERT AUTHORIZED
  t=150 ap applies UPDATE CAPTURED
  final: eu=CAPTURED  us=CAPTURED  ap=CAPTURED

Discarding leaves the regions apart for good. Timestamps make them agree, but on the version without the capture, and even us ignores its own capture because its stamp is older. With the clock 60 ms ahead instead, the timestamps run ends eu=CAPTURED us=CAPTURED ap=CAPTURED (ap ignores the late insert: ts 0 < 105). Same events, opposite outcome: timestamps are right only when the clocks happen to agree with the order of events. The causal run is right whatever the clocks say.

sections.h: Handling a conflict: avoid it, let the last write win, or keep both
sections.html:
Two writes conflict when neither leader had seen the other's write when it accepted its own. The clock doesn't decide it. Two laptops that edit a merchant record offline, an hour apart, conflict. Two writes 2 ms apart don't, if the second one's leader had already applied the first. Lesson 8 makes this precise as the happens-before relation. There are three ways to handle a conflict, and one kind of rule that none of them can save.

The cheapest is to avoid it. Give every record a home region and send all its writes there. M-0042 is homed in eu, so a terminal in Virginia that writes M-0042's holds goes to the eu leader and pays the round trip, while most traffic, which is local, stays fast. The rule breaks when the home moves: eu fails and us takes M-0042's writes, or the merchant moves its business. For that window, two leaders write the same rows. IDs need the same care. Two leaders that both hand out the next value of one sequence will issue the same number twice, which is why pgactive's README lists "the lack of certain convenient database features such as incremental integer sequences" among the things an application must handle. Use per-region ranges, or UUIDs.

The second is to let the last write win. Every change carries a timestamp, and every leader keeps the higher one. The leaders converge, and one of two concurrent writes disappears with no error. DynamoDB global tables do this per item in their default mode, and pgactive does it for INSERT/INSERT and UPDATE/UPDATE conflicts, keeping the row with the newest timestamp from its origin. How much it loses depends on how often two regions write the same row within the replication lag. In this lesson's lab, two regions add holds to one merchant with 20 to 80 ms of lag. With writes 5 s apart in each region, 1% of acknowledged holds vanish; 300 ms apart, 12.5%; 50 ms apart, 38.5%. Last write wins is safe only when each key is written once, such as inserts with unique ids.

The third is to keep both and merge. Each change records which writes its leader had seen. A leader that receives a change it can't order against its own keeps both versions, as siblings, and the next reader merges them. Holds are only ever added, so taking the union is a correct merge here, and the lab's detector loses nothing at any rate. Deletes are harder, because a union brings removed items back; lesson 8 fixes that with CRDTs. The merge can also be your own code that runs on each conflict. pgactive's docs describe a custom conflict handler next to last update wins, though the same docs call user-defined conflict handling planned, so check the version you run.

Some rules no merge can repair. Two regions each approve a 600 payment against a balance of 1,000, and each was right about its own copy. Keeping both writes breaks the rule; dropping one throws away a payment the customer was told was approved. A rule like that needs the regions to agree before the write commits, which is what the next section's synchronous products do.

try.title: How loss depends on how often two regions write
steps: ContentionDemo.kt runs the lab's setup: two regions, 300 holds added in each, 20 to 80 ms of lag, once with last write wins and once with the conflict detector, for six write rates.
Predict the share lost under last write wins when each region writes every 300 ms on average. Then run it.
Run it with another seed, -Pargs='7', and check which numbers move.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l05.demo.ContentionDemoKt -q ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.repl.l05.demo.ContentionDemoKt -Pargs='7' -q

try.expect:
600 acknowledged writes (300 per region), lag 20 to 80 ms, seed 42
mean gap between writes   last write wins lost   detector lost
     5,000 ms per region       6  ( 1.0%)             0
     1,000 ms per region      23  ( 3.8%)             0
       300 ms per region      75  (12.5%)             0
       100 ms per region     158  (26.3%)             0
        50 ms per region     231  (38.5%)             0
        10 ms per region     330  (55.0%)             0

The loss rate follows contention: the more often both regions write the same row inside one lag window, the more writes last write wins throws away. It never reaches zero, because even at one write every 5 seconds two writes sometimes land within 80 ms of each other. With seed 7 the rows read 0.7%, 4.2%, 12.2%, 26.3%, 37.8% and 51.0%: the rates are a property of the workload, not luck. The detector column stays at 0 for every seed. Every run takes well under a second, because time in the simulation is virtual.

sections.h: Multi-region products: who takes writes for a row, and does the write wait
sections.html:
Most products sold as multi-region aren't multi-leader in this lesson's sense. Ask two questions of each one. How many places accept a write for the same row? And does a write wait for another region before it commits?

waits for another region doesn't wait
one writer per row CockroachDB (Raft per range) Aurora Global Database
several writers per row DynamoDB global tables, MRSC; MySQL Group Replication, multi-primary DynamoDB global tables, MREC; pgactive

Aurora Global Database has one primary region that takes writes, and read-only secondaries fed asynchronously. A planned switchover waits for the chosen secondary to catch up, so it loses nothing. An unplanned failover can lose whatever hadn't crossed yet, an RPO (recovery point objective: how much recent data you may lose) that AWS says is "typically measured in seconds". Write forwarding lets an app in a secondary region send writes, but they still go to the one writer.

CockroachDB replicates each range of rows with Raft (the Consistency and consensus track covers it), so one replica, the leaseholder, orders each range's writes. A REGIONAL BY ROW table keeps each row's home region in a hidden crdb_region column and partitions by it, so rows homed in your region get fast consistent reads and writes. That's this lesson's conflict avoidance by home region, built into the database. Surviving the loss of a whole region needs at least three regions, raises the replication factor from 3 to 5, and adds at least one round trip to the nearest region to every write.

DynamoDB global tables choose a mode at creation, for good. MREC (multi-Region eventual consistency, the default) is true multi-leader: it replicates "typically within a second or less", and per item the last writer wins. The docs spell out what follows. A strongly consistent read can return stale data if the item was last written in another Region; a conditional write checks only its own Region's copy; a transaction is atomic only in the Region that ran it. MRSC (multi-Region strong consistency) replicates each write to at least one other Region before returning, so a strongly consistent read anywhere sees the latest version. It asks a lot in return: exactly three Regions (three replicas, or two and a witness that holds data but serves no requests), created from an empty table, no replicas added later, and no TTL, local secondary indexes or transactions. A write to an item that another Region is modifying fails with ReplicatedWriteConflictException, and you retry.

MySQL Group Replication in multi-primary mode lets up to 9 members take writes and certifies each transaction against concurrent ones from other members. When two touch the same row, the one ordered first commits everywhere and the other rolls back, "a distributed first commit wins rule" in the manual's words. Every commit waits for the group to agree on an order, and the limits are sharp: SERIALIZABLE is refused, cascading foreign keys aren't supported, and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks aren't shared across members.

For money, give each row one writer at a time, by home region or by consensus. Keep last write wins for data where losing one of two concurrent writes costs nothing.

try.title: One retried checkout under MREC and MRSC rules
steps: Read the comment at the top of IdempotencyDemo.kt. It is a toy model of the two modes as the DynamoDB docs describe them, not DynamoDB itself.
Predict how many times the card is charged under each mode, then run it.
try.expect:
-- MREC (eventual): the condition is checked against the local Region's copy --
t=0    eu condition passes, card charged (charge #1)
t=200  us condition passes, card charged (charge #2)
t=900  both copies converge on one item: us-result
charges: 2 for one checkout

-- MRSC (strong): writes replicate synchronously; a racing write fails --
t=0    eu condition passes, card charged (charge #1), write returns at t=250
t=200  us ReplicatedWriteConflictException: item is being modified in another Region
t=300  us ConditionalCheckFailed: replay the stored result
charges: 1 for one checkout

Under MREC, attribute_not_exists was true in both Regions, because us hadn't received eu's item yet. Both charged, and last writer wins later keeps one item, which hides the evidence. Under MRSC the retry ran into the first write while it was still replicating, got ReplicatedWriteConflictException, retried 100 ms later, found the key and replayed the stored result. The price is visible too: the eu write took 250 ms to return, because it waited for another Region.

refs.title: Amazon DynamoDB: how global tables work (MREC and MRSC)
MySQL 8.4: Group Replication background (certification, first commit wins)
Aurora Global Database: switchover and failover

analogy: Two branches of a bank each keep a full copy of the customer ledger, and every evening each posts the other a list of the day's entries. Customers never wait for the other branch, and if the post is late, both branches keep working. Trouble comes when both branches changed the same customer's page on the same day: the lists arrive, and each clerk finds an entry that doesn't fit what they wrote. They can agree that the entry with the later time stamp wins (and lose the other), keep both and phone the customer, or agree in advance that each customer belongs to one branch. A rule like "never below zero" can't be checked by either clerk alone. The analogy breaks on speed and scale: real leaders exchange thousands of changes a second, nobody reads them, and the conflict rule has to be chosen before the first conflict happens.
world: Your Oracle ledger has one primary taking every write, and a Data Guard standby in another region waits, read-only. That is Aurora Global's shape: one writer, asynchronous copies, a failover that may lose the last seconds. If someone proposes active-active for the payments API, ask which tables would be written in both regions. Idempotency keys and balances can't be: each region would check uniqueness and limits against its own copy, and a retried checkout would charge twice. Give those a home region per merchant or a store that agrees before it commits. Kafka has met the loop problem too: MirrorMaker 2 renames a replicated topic with its source cluster's alias (eu.payments in the us cluster), so it never copies a topic back to where it came from.
mistake: The most common mistake is turning on a second writable region for a table that holds money and expecting it to behave like one database. People do it because the console makes it one setting and the latency graphs improve the same day. Then a retried checkout lands in the other region within the replication lag, both regions pass the idempotency check against their own copy, and the card is charged twice; or one of two concurrent balance updates disappears under last write wins, with no error anywhere. The fix is to decide table by table. Rows that move money get one writer at a time, through a home region or a store that agrees before committing (DynamoDB MRSC, CockroachDB), and the code retries ReplicatedWriteConflictException. Last write wins is for data where losing one of two concurrent writes is acceptable, such as a merchant's display name.

compare.title: Two Regions, one retried checkout: the two DynamoDB global table modes

a.label: MREC (eventual, the default)
a.title: MREC (eventual, the default)
a.html:
eu  t=0    put idem-7f3a if attribute_not_exists   -> OK (checks eu's copy)
us  t=200  put idem-7f3a if attribute_not_exists   -> OK (us hasn't seen eu's item)
           two charges
later      replication: last writer wins per item  -> one item survives

write latency: local
RPO: the replication delay, usually a few seconds

b.label: MRSC (strong, exactly 3 Regions)
b.title: MRSC (strong, exactly 3 Regions)
b.html:
eu  t=0    put idem-7f3a if attribute_not_exists   -> OK after another Region has it
us  t=200  put idem-7f3a                           -> ReplicatedWriteConflictException
us  t=300  retry                                   -> ConditionalCheckFailed: replay
           one charge

write latency: at least one cross-Region round trip
RPO: 0; no TTL, no LSIs, no transactions

compare.note: Both modes accept writes in every Region; the difference is when they find out about each other. MREC finds out after both writes committed, so it can only pick a winner, and a condition is only as good as the local copy it checked. MRSC finds out before the write returns, so it can refuse one of them and let the caller retry against the latest version. That costs a cross-Region round trip on every write and rules out features that need local, asynchronous work.

worked.title: Put a payments API in two regions without double charges

steps.say: List each table, where its writes come from, and what one lost concurrent write would mean. Be concrete.
steps.code:
table              written from         lose one of two concurrent writes?
idempotency_keys   any region           a double charge
balances           any region           money moves twice or not at all
merchant_profile   back office, rare    a stale display name for a while
holds              terminals, constant  an authorization hold forgotten

steps.say: Home every merchant in one region and route its money writes there. A request in the other region pays one round trip for that merchant only.
steps.code: fun writerFor(merchant: Merchant): DataSource = if (merchant.homeRegion == localRegion) localLeader // about 1 ms else leaders.getValue(merchant.homeRegion) // about 70 ms, but one writer per row

steps.say: Stop leaders handing out the same ids. PostgreSQL 18 generates time-ordered UUIDs, so ids from both regions never collide and still sort roughly by time.
steps.code: CREATE TABLE holds ( id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(), merchant_id text NOT NULL, amount_minor bigint NOT NULL );

steps.say: Write down what happens when a home region is down. Either refuse money writes for its merchants until it returns (one writer, some downtime), or move their home and accept that rows written in both places during the switch will conflict. Pick per table, before the outage.
steps.code:
eu down, merchant homed in eu:
  idempotency_keys, balances -> refuse: 503 for those merchants
  merchant_profile           -> accept in us; last write wins when eu returns
  holds                      -> accept in us; insert-only with uuidv7 ids, nothing to conflict

steps.say: Measure conflicts instead of guessing. With pgactive, set pgactive.log_conflicts_to_table to true and count what lands in its history table; any conflict on a money table is a routing bug.
steps.code: SELECT count(*) FROM pgactive.pgactive_conflict_history;

lab.title: Two regions, last write wins, and a conflict detector
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. All 11 fail with NotImplementedError.

Read Regions.kt, which is given. Each region is a leader for merchant M-0042's holds; simulate runs writes and replication on virtual time, with a random delay per message, so messages overtake each other and a minute of traffic runs in milliseconds. Every write records in seen the ids of all writes its region knew about.

In Conflicts.kt, write lastWriteWins. Its test and the two last-write-wins simulations pass. Read the steady-traffic test: 600 acknowledged writes, more than 150 of them lost, and the regions still agree.
Write order from the seen sets alone. Never look at the timestamps.
Write applyDetecting. The rest pass, including the clock-skew test and a jqwik property that tries random seeds with two to four regions and checks that nothing is ever lost.
Experiment: make order use timestamps instead (a.timestamp < b.timestamp means BEFORE). See which tests fail, and why. Put it back.
hints: compareValuesBy(a, b, Write::timestamp, Write::region) compares by timestamp, then by region name.
order is a when with four branches: SAME first, then a.id in b.seen, then b.id in a.seen, then CONCURRENT.
In applyDetecting, an incoming write that is SAME as or BEFORE any current version changes nothing.
Otherwise keep current.filter { order(it, incoming) == Order.CONCURRENT }, add incoming, and report a conflict when that filtered list isn't empty.
Region.read() returns the union of the siblings' holds. That union is the application's merge.

drill.title: Three regions and four rules, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking: (a) sketch three leaders in all-to-all and the timeline in which an UPDATE reaches the third region before its INSERT; (b) list what discarding, last write wins and causal holding each do with it; (c) name the four ways to handle a conflict and what each one costs; (d) fill the 2x2 of one or several writers per row against waits or doesn't wait for another region, with one product in each cell.

answer.html:
(a) eu --INSERT--> us (fast)  eu --INSERT--> ap (slow)
    us applies INSERT, then UPDATE --> ap (fast): ap sees UPDATE first
(b) discard: ap keeps the INSERT's row, regions disagree forever
    last write wins: agree, but a slow clock can make the UPDATE lose everywhere
    hold until what the UPDATE's origin had seen is applied: right answer, any clocks
(c) avoid (home region): breaks when the home moves; ids need ranges or UUIDs
    last write wins: converges, silently drops one of two concurrent writes
    keep siblings and merge: no loss, but someone must merge; deletes need CRDTs
    agree before commit: no conflicts, a cross-region round trip per write
(d)                      waits                       doesn't wait
    one writer per row   CockroachDB                 Aurora Global Database
    several writers      DynamoDB MRSC, MySQL GR     DynamoDB MREC, pgactive

recap: Multi-leader replication puts a leader in each region (or device): writes commit locally in about a millisecond and replicate asynchronously to the other leaders, so a region or a link can fail without stopping writes.

The cost is conflicts: two leaders accept writes to the same row before either has seen the other's. Rules that must see every write, such as a unique idempotency key or a balance at zero or above, can only be checked against a local copy.

Topologies: circles and stars depend on single nodes; all-to-all doesn't, but changes overtake each other, so an UPDATE can reach a region before its INSERT. Origin ids stop loops; timestamps can't order the changes, and recording what each change had seen can.

Handle conflicts by avoiding them (a home region per record), last write wins (converges and silently loses: 1% to 55% of acknowledged writes in the lab, depending on contention), or keeping siblings and merging. Invariants need agreement before commit.

Products: Aurora Global has one asynchronous writer; CockroachDB orders each range with Raft and homes rows with REGIONAL BY ROW; DynamoDB MREC is last-writer-wins per item with local conditional checks; MRSC waits for another Region, needs exactly three, and rejects racing writes; MySQL Group Replication certifies and lets the first-ordered transaction win.

explain.prompt: A product manager asks why the team can't just switch the payments table in DynamoDB to write in both regions, since the latency graphs would improve. Explain what happens to two concurrent writes and to a conditional write, and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: In the default mode, MREC, each region commits writes locally and replicates them within about a second. If both regions update the same item inside that second, neither knew about the other, and when the copies meet DynamoDB keeps the one with the later internal timestamp and drops the other without an error. Conditional writes don't protect us either, because each region checks the condition against its own copy: a retried checkout with the same idempotency key passes attribute_not_exists in both regions and charges twice, and a transaction is only atomic in the region that ran it. For tables that move money I'd give every merchant a home region and send its money writes there, or use MRSC, which waits for another region before returning and fails a racing write with ReplicatedWriteConflictException so we can retry. MRSC costs a cross-region round trip per write and needs exactly three regions, with no transactions or TTL. Data where losing one of two concurrent writes is harmless, like display names, can use MREC and keep the latency win.

deeper.html:
GitHub's October 2018 outage shows what happens when a single-leader system acts like a multi-leader one for a few minutes. A 43-second network partition between data centers on the US East Coast led its failover tooling to promote primaries in US West, and applications wrote there for about 40 minutes, while the East primaries still held several seconds of writes that had never replicated. Each side now had writes the other lacked, so failing back was not safe, and East-coast applications couldn't tolerate a cross-country round trip on most queries. Degraded service lasted 24 hours and 11 minutes. The write-up is worth reading in full for how the team reasoned about which writes to keep: https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/oct21-post-incident-analysis/

pgactive descends from BDR (Bi-Directional Replication), a PostgreSQL extension built on logical decoding, and the same ideas survive in commercial PostgreSQL distributions. Its conflict documentation is a useful catalogue even if you never run it: it lists INSERT/INSERT, UPDATE/UPDATE, UPDATE/DELETE, INSERT/UPDATE (the overtaking case), foreign key and exclusion constraint conflicts, and explains why it refuses exclusion constraints altogether: on fully isolated nodes, no one can guarantee that no two rows overlap.

The second edition of Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann and Riccomini), chapter 6, covers multi-leader topologies, conflict avoidance, convergence and the sync engines of lesson 6 in more depth, and points to the papers behind them. Lesson 8 of this track picks up the thread with version vectors and CRDTs, the tools that make "keep both and merge" practical.
